newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian GDP growth seen at 3.5 pct in 97 - PECC.
newsitem.headline: Australian GDP growth seen at 3.5 pct in 97 - PECC.

text.p: Australia's real gross domestic product (GDP) growth is forecast to slow to 3.5 percent in calendar 1997 from four percent in 1996, the Pacific Economic Cooperation Council (PECC) said on Tuesday.

This reflects the balance between slower growth in private consumption, totalling three percent, and business investment, of 9.8 percent, a deterioration in net trade volumes and a seven percent recovery in housing investment, the PECC said in its 1997/98 Pacific Economic Outlook.
It forecast net trade volumes to slide to a deficit of about 0.1 percent of GDP from a surplus of 0.7 percent in 1996.

Despite the Federal government's expenditure cuts in 1997, the PECC said it expects a positive contribution to growth from government spending due to offsetting increases in state government investment expenditure.
Australian import volume growth is forecast to rise to 9.8 percent in 1997 from 8.5 percent growth in 1996 mainly as a result of an increase in the real exchange rate, it said.
Export volume growth is expected to fall for the same reason.

The deterioration in net trade volumes, coupled with little expected change in the terms of trade, is expected to lead to a widening of the current account deficit, both in U.S. dollars and as a percentage of GDP, the PECC said.
In 1996, the current account deficit averaged 3.7 percent of GDP, down from 5.3 percent in 1995, due entirely to a shift into surplus in the trade balance, it said.

It forecast a further fall in consumer price index inflation in 1997 to 1.8 percent from 2.6 percent in 1996, based on the assumption four percent growth in average weekly earnings will keep real wages adjusted for productivity roughly unchanged.
"Our optimism on wages reflects the current high level of unemployment, which gives unions little scope for negotiating increases in real wage rates," the PECC said.
For 1998, it forecast a rise in real GDP growth to four percent, an improvement in the current account deficit to 3.8 percent of GDP and a rise in CPI inflation.
